source: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 8 (Peasants, Zamindars and the State).

sections.heading: 1. Agrarian Society under the Mughals
points: The chapter studies **agrarian relations (16th–17th c.)** under the **Mughal Empire**.
The main source is the **'Ain-i-Akbari'** by **Abul Fazl** (a detailed record of Akbar's administration, revenue, and society).
The basic unit of society was the **village**; the peasant was called a **raiyat (or muzarian)**.

sections.heading: 2. Peasants and Agriculture
points: Two kinds of peasants: **khud-kashta** (resident cultivators of the village) and **pahi-kashta** (non-resident, from other villages).
Agriculture was intensive; crops classified as **kharif (autumn) and rabi (spring)**; cash crops ('jins-i kamil' — cotton, sugarcane) were grown.
**Irrigation** and technology (Persian wheel, wooden plough) supported farming; new crops (maize, tomato, potato, chillies from the Americas) were introduced.

sections.heading: 3. Zamindars and Village Community
points: **Zamindars** — landed proprietors who enjoyed high status, held their own lands (milkiyat), and **collected revenue** on behalf of the state (keeping a share); often had armed retainers.
The **village panchayat** and the headman (**muqaddam/mandal**) managed village affairs; the **patwari** kept records.
The **jajmani** system and caste-based occupations organised rural life; women played a vital role in production.

sections.heading: 4. Land Revenue and the Mansabdari System
points: **Land revenue** was the economic backbone of the Mughal state; the **diwan** oversaw revenue.
**Todar Mal's revenue system (zabt/dahsala)** under Akbar — assessment based on measured land, average yields and prices; revenue fixed in cash.
The **jama** (assessed amount) and **hasil** (collected amount); **mansabdars** and **jagirdars** were assigned revenue rights (jagirs) for service.
The **Ain-i-Akbari** documents the empire's revenue and administrative structure.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Main source = Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl (Akbar's administration).
Peasant = raiyat; khud-kashta (resident) vs pahi-kashta (non-resident).
Zamindars collected revenue and held milkiyat lands (high status).
Todar Mal's zabt/dahsala system = measured land revenue in cash.
Village head = muqaddam/mandal; record-keeper = patwari.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: The **Ain-i-Akbari** was written by **Abul Fazl** (part of the Akbarnama).
**Khud-kashta = resident cultivators; pahi-kashta = non-resident** (from other villages).
**Todar Mal** designed the **zabt/dahsala** revenue system under Akbar.
**Zamindars collected revenue** for the state and kept a share (they were not simply landless).
